title: Machinae
summary: The devices built by Enlightened craftsmen of the Renaissance.

claims.text: Machinae balance on the edge of plausibility, built by flawless logic and astrological design yet often fantastic in result.
Nearly all their makers belong to the Order of Reason, whose principles of mathematics, innovation and materialism they embody; only a few Disparate eccentrics build them otherwise.

title: Daedalean craft ranks
summary: How the Order of Reason's craftsmen rank themselves.

claims.text: Artisans use apprentice everywhere, treat mediator, artisan and journeyman as one rank, and resplendent and master as another; Artificers add Facilitators, Magistrates, Grand Artisans and Epitomes because they span many cities.
The Craftmasons are both more democratic and more hierarchical, with 33 levels, and many refuse to see a real gap between Enlightened and ordinary Brethren.

title: Masters the Artisans honour
summary: The ancient and medieval inventors Daedaleans look back to.

claims.text: Some Artificers prefer Archytas of Tarentum, who built flying automatons, to Pythagoras; Archimedes, whose war machines held off Rome at Syracuse for three years, is held the greatest of the Greeks.
The Tower of the Winds in Athens, with its water-clocks and sundials, is seen as a building-sized Machina for the study of Time.
Roger Bacon's influence among the High Artisans remains immense; the Craftmasons showed their strength in 1210 when they brought down Mistridge with cannon.

title: Infernal Lithuania
summary: A pagan land where the powers of Hell hold sway.

claims.text: Lithuania's conversion was royal politics; bloody paganism stays strong, and the country holds off the Teutonic Knights by alliance with Poland.
Appa Bloodax and the even worse Tezghul the Insane rank as senior chiefs, but their real power comes from Hell.

title: Ars Praeclarus
summary: The Daedalean belief that reason can grasp all creation.

claims.text: The Ars Praeclarus is the practical working of a philosophy: the world can be analysed, to understand a thing is to have power over it, and human reason can take in everything.
Hermetic magi share the love of measurement and may be fussier still.
